body.text: In short:
The Greens want the government to commit to reforming charity rules in exchange for passage of its tax bills.
A "name and shame" proposal for trusts and beneficiaries is not a red line and the Greens have no major issues with the government's CGT carve-out.
What's next?
The government is trying to pass two tax bills through the Senate by the end of next week.
The Greens could pass Labor's two major tax bills by the end of next week if the minor party can extract a promise to reform the charities sector.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants parliament's support for legislation to impose a minimum tax on some trusts and to carve out start-ups from the new capital gains tax (CGT) regime.
The Coalition is opposed, making the Greens the only viable pathway in the Senate.
The minor party is comfortable with the principle of both measures and would support them subject to a small number of changes, several Greens sources told the ABC.

The party's red line is an exemption for private schools and other non-tax-paying recipients, which they want repealed along with a commitment to consider broader charitable sector reform, including the tax treatment of religious institutions.

But the Greens have no apparent red lines on the CGT start-up carve-out and appear unlikely to support independent MP Allegra Spender's proposed alternative, despite expressing openness to it yesterday.
Mr Chalmers revealed this morning that he had written to Ms Spender outlining Treasury's concerns with her proposal.
That letter, seen by the ABC, said her idea would be "neither simple nor straightforward" and would be inequitable.
Spender proposal not 'fairer', Chalmers says

The CGT issue relates to a workaround the government devised in response to a complaint from start-ups that the new inflation-based discount would unfairly penalise them, because they start from scratch and so had no cost base to be "inflated".

The government's proposed concession would apply to businesses less than 15 years old, subject to a test to establish whether they were developing or commercialising "genuinely innovative products, processes, services or methods".

Ms Spender said the exemption was too narrow and subjective and that any "active" business assets should instead get a 40 per cent discount, which she said would raise a similar amount of money but be simpler.
In his letter to Ms Spender, Mr Chalmers said Treasury had "identified a number of issues and concerns".
"Their analysis suggests that your proposal is unlikely to be simpler, fairer or enhance productivity, as you suggest," he wrote.

"Your proposal would introduce a second set of tax arrangements for capital gains and replaces one arbitrary distortion in the tax system with another, for the majority of assets. [It] risks introducing more complexity, not less."

In the letter, Mr Chalmers said early-stage start-ups, which were most likely to be innovative, would likely stand to pay higher taxes under the 40 per cent idea and that identifying which assets were "active" would be complex.

"This would need to occur regularly and across all businesses to ensure shareholders understand an entity's status, as opposed to the current definition that only applies to small businesses in years where CGT events arise," he wrote.
He added that the proposal could "introduce pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", such as by putting properties and other assets into an "active" business vehicle to pay less tax.
Call to listen to business

In a statement, Ms Spender told the ABC her proposal was "gathering wide support in the business community" and reiterated her call to the government to "listen seriously to what business is saying and carefully analyse and evaluate the advantages" of her model.
"I would welcome a thorough and serious parliamentary inquiry," she said.

Ms Spender added that she "appreciated" the letter but that it had "failed to recognise the concerns of the business community" with the existing approach "and its real-world impacts on risk-taking and investment...
"The business community wasn't consulted on the government's original CGT direction but is willing to compromise. The government should be willing to listen now."

Greens sources told the ABC the party had no particular inclination to support Ms Spender's proposal, saying that Senator McKim's suggestion yesterday that he was "open" to it should not be read as an endorsement.
The sources said the minor party was broadly supportive of the idea of giving innovative start-ups the option to choose between the old 50 per cent discount and the new discount.

The Greens opted not to support a Coalition motion today to refer the bill, which also includes research and development tax incentive changes and changes to the EV discount, to a Senate inquiry reporting in the new year.
But the minor party is keeping its options open on that front and sees no urgency to pass either of the tax bills by the end of the year if the government is unwilling to give ground.
Charitable exemption for trusts under microscope

On trusts, the Greens' sole concern is that an exemption for charitable giving is too broad, allowing people to escape the 30 per cent tax not just by giving to registered charities but to any income tax-exempt entity, including private schools and sporting clubs.

Senator McKim, the party's economic spokesperson, used a Senate inquiry into the bill to recommend this be restricted to registered charities only, and that the government agree to respond to a 2024 Productivity Commission report into charity rules.

That report found the granting of "deductible gift recipient" and tax-exempt status to non-charities had "no coherent policy rationale". It advocated excluding private and religious schools and religious activities.
A Greens source emphasised that the government would not necessarily need to agree to go this far, but that there was appetite to see the issue probed.
Recent scrutiny over the election activity of Exclusive Brethren church members was cited as a motivator.
The source said another recommendation from the inquiry, to facilitate a public register of trusts and their beneficiaries, was not a red line for negotiations.
No rush to pass by end of year
Sources said there had been no tangible progress to report on any concessions.
When the Greens' concerns about private schools were first reported by the ABC last month, Mr Chalmers said he had learned of the concern from the reporting.

"I haven't had the opportunity to engage directly … we've tried to make sure that there are reasonable arrangements for charities, for not-for-profits, which reflect some of the current arrangements that are in place," he told Radio National at the time.
"There are good reasons for those sorts of exemptions. [Private school giving] is a very specific sliver of what's being proposed here."
